intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene on chromosome 17.

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Testing the Mariana Islands pedigree for TMEM98 mutations identified a 34 bp heterozygous deletion that spans the 3' end of exon 4 in all affected family members.
checks.explanation: Paper reports TMEM98 mutations (heterozygous deletion; dominant missense) causing autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.

checks.claim: The TMEM98 gene is located on chromosome 17.
checks.evidence_quote: Significant linkage was detected on chromosome 17 between single-nucleotide polymorphism markers rs2323659 and rs967293, with a maximum location score of 4.1. Exome sequencing identified a single novel segregating missense variant within the linkage region located in exon 8 of the transmembrane-98 (TMEM98) gene
checks.explanation: TMEM98 lies in the chromosome 17 linkage region.

paragraphs.text: Nanophthalmos is a congenital disorder in which the eyes are small but structurally normal. Its main complications are severe hyperopia and angle-closure glaucoma (Awadalla et al., 2014). Patients also have a higher risk of complications after eye surgery (Khorram et al., 2015). The form described in this entry is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

checks.evidence_quote: Patients with nanophthalmos have high hyperopia (far-sightedness), a greater incidence of angle-closure glaucoma, and increased risk of surgical complications.

paragraphs.text: Yu et al. (2009) studied a 5-generation Chinese family in which isolated microphthalmia was inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Nine affected members, aged 6 to 66 years (mean, 42.8 years), had bilateral microphthalmia present from birth and no other physical anomalies. Hyperopia ranged from +4.50 to +11.50 diopters (mean, +8.00 diopters). Axial length ranged from 18.22 mm to 20.26 mm (mean, 19.29 mm). Best corrected visual acuity was less than 0.5 in most eyes. Three patients, all older than 50 years, had angle-closure glaucoma or occludable anterior chamber angles. They were treated with trabeculectomy, but the disease continued to progress, and 2 of them developed atrophia bulbi despite repeated surgeries. Histologic examination of the sclera showed diffusely swollen collagen fibers that were twisted or frayed and mixed with normal fibers. In the atrophied globes, the alignment of collagen fibers was disrupted, the sclera contained many coil-like amorphous materials and was 3 times the normal thickness, and the corneas were also thickened. The authors also noted learning disabilities in one-third of the cases. Karyotypes were normal in all 9 affected members.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied a large white family (NNO-SA1) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos, recruited in South Australia. They defined nanophthalmos as an axial length of less than 20.0 mm and/or a refractive error greater than +7.00. paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) reported 2 large pedigrees with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Inheritance was highly penetrant and spanned at least 4 generations in each. In a Caucasian family of German heritage living in the United States (pedigree 991-F), 6 of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, and 3 more were affected according to family history. Affected members had a mean axial eye length of 17.1 +/- 0.31 mm and spherical equivalent refractions of +13.0 +/- 0.89 diopters, compared with +0.71 +/- 0.81 diopters in unaffected members. In a Pacific Islander family of Micronesian heritage living in the Mariana Islands (pedigree 951-N), 8 of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, and 3 more were affected according to family history. Affected members had a mean axial eye length of 17.4 +/- 0.94 mm, compared with 22.7 +/- 0.38 mm in unaffected members, and spherical equivalent refractions of +3.93 +/- 1.57 diopters. Across the patients with nanophthalmos, axial eye lengths ranged from 15.9 to 18.4 mm.

paragraphs.text: Hu et al. (2011) carried out a genomewide scan with 382 microsatellite markers in a Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital simple microphthalmia, after excluding the candidate loci previously reported. The highest lod score was 4.97 at D17S1824 (theta = 0.00). Haplotype analysis placed the disease gene in a 21.57-cM interval between D17S900 and D17S1872 on chromosome 17p12-q12. Sequencing of 14 candidate genes, including CRYBA1 and NCOR1, found no mutation, and genomewide SNP genotyping found no pathogenic copy number variation.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian family from the United States with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (pedigree 991-F), Khorram et al. (2015) performed exome sequencing within the regions linked to the disease. This identified a his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed that all other affected family members carried the mutation, and it was absent from healthy family members. Of the 4 nonsynonymous variants found in the chromosome 17 critical region, H196P was the only one that both segregated with the disease and was predicted to be pathogenic by SIFT, PolyPhen, and BLOSUM62. The affected histidine is highly conserved across species. In a Pacific Islander family from the Mariana Islands with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (pedigree 951-N), the authors found a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in TMEM98 in all affected family members; it was absent from healthy family members. The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4, removing a splice site, and is predicted to cause premature termination of translation. Neither mutation was present in the Exome Variant Server or 1000 Genomes Project databases.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large white family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (NNO4) linked to chromosome 17p12-q12, Awadalla et al. (2014) identified a c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene, resulting in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and was the only novel segregating variant in the linked region. It was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls.

checks.evidence_quote: Exome sequencing identified a single novel segregating missense variant within the linkage region located in exon 8 of the transmembrane-98 (TMEM98) gene c.577G>C (p.Ala193Pro)
checks.explanation: A G>C change is a transversion, and a segregating variant is by definition present in affected members.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a Caucasian family from the United States with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (NNO4) (pedigree 991-F), Khorram et al. (2015) identified a his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It segregated with the disease, was absent from healthy family members and from the Exome Variant Server and 1000 Genomes Project databases, and affected a highly conserved histidine. SIFT, PolyPhen, and BLOSUM62 all predicted it to be pathogenic.

checks.claim: Khorram et al. (2015) identified a his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene in affected members of pedigree 991-F, a Caucasian family from the United States with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (NNO4).
checks.evidence_quote: a His196Pro mutation was detected in the TMEM98 gene, which was recently reported to be a nanophthalmos gene. Sanger sequencing subsequently showed that all other members of this pedigree with nanophthalmos also carry the His196Pro TMEM98 mutation.

checks.claim: The TMEM98 H196P mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
checks.evidence_quote: Genes within these "linked regions" were examined for disease-causing mutations using exome sequencing, and a His196Pro mutation was detected in the TMEM98 gene
checks.explanation: The abstract also says Sanger sequencing confirmed it in the other affected members.

paragraphs.text: In all affected members of a Pacific Islander family from the Mariana Islands with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos (NNO4) (pedigree 951-N), Khorram et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in the TMEM98 gene (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg). The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4. It removes a splice site and is predicted to cause premature termination of translation. The deletion was absent from healthy family members and from the Exome Variant Server and 1000 Genomes Project databases.
